lead: A security policy turns business rules into enforceable controls. Risk management decides which controls are worth their cost. A bank, a hospital or a UPI payment app cannot protect everything equally, so it ranks assets, threats and weaknesses, then chooses avoid, reduce, transfer or accept. Audit and monitoring produce evidence that the controls work. This chapter links policy hierarchy, risk scores, legal duties and audit practice into one management loop. It uses a simple annual loss calculation to show why a control may be rejected even when it improves security.
prereq: You need: access control policy and Unit 1 threats and vulnerabilities.

blocks.text: A security policy is a management statement of intent. It says what must be protected and what behaviour is allowed. A standard is a mandatory, measurable rule that supports a policy, such as “all customer passwords must be stored using a salted one-way function”. A procedure is the ordered steps staff follow to meet a standard. A guideline is recommended advice; it is not mandatory. The hierarchy matters because auditors test standards and procedures, not slogans.

Policies fail when they are vague. “Protect data” cannot be enforced. “Remote access must use multi-factor authentication” can be enforced and audited. For example, access control policy names subjects, objects, operations and the model used for decisions.

Write the policy first, then the standards that make it testable. Add procedures for routine work: onboarding, key rotation, incident escalation. Keep guidelines short so people read them. Review all four levels after a major change, such as a new UPI service or a data-sharing contract.

Risk management starts with an asset: anything of value, such as a database, a laptop or a customer list. A threat is a possible cause of harm, such as a phishing gang or a power cut. A vulnerability is a weakness that a threat can exploit, such as an unpatched server. Likelihood is the chance that the threat exploits the weakness in a period. Impact is the loss if it happens. Risk combines both; it is not the same as threat or vulnerability alone.

blocks.where: likelihood and impact are integers from 1 to 5; the risk score ranges from 1 to 25, as shown in the matrix.

blocks.text: Treatment has four choices: avoid the activity, reduce the risk with controls, transfer it (for example insurance), or accept it with management sign-off. A control costs money and staff time, so compare its yearly saving with its yearly cost. If the saving is smaller, the simple business case rejects the control.

blocks.where: SLE is single loss expectancy in rupees; exposure factor is the fraction of asset value lost in one event.

blocks.text: ALE = SLE × annualised rate of occurrence
blocks.where: ALE is annualised loss expectancy in rupees per year; annualised rate of occurrence is events per year.

blocks.text: A risk register lists each risk with owner, score, treatment, cost and review date. It is the working memory of the programme. Security programme drivers include legal duty, contracts with customers, business continuity and past incidents. A regulator or a large client can require evidence, so the programme must produce records, not just controls.

ISO 27001 defines requirements for an information security management system (ISMS). ISO 27005 gives risk management guidance. Laws are narrower: FISMA 2002 covers US federal agencies; GLBA covers US financial institutions; HIPAA covers US health information. These laws require safeguards and evidence, but compliance alone does not prove security.

Audit checks whether controls exist and operate. Logging records events; monitoring watches them; compliance evidence includes tickets, approvals, logs and test reports. A vulnerability assessment finds weaknesses; a penetration test safely attempts exploitation. Cloud shared responsibility shifts some controls to the provider, as covered in cloud security services.

examples.question: An asset is worth ₹10,00,000. A threat exploits a vulnerability with exposure factor 25% and annualised rate of occurrence 0.2 per year. (a) Compute single loss expectancy. (b) Compute annualised loss expectancy. (c) A control costs ₹60,000 per year and reduces ALE to ₹20,000. Is it cost-effective by the simple ALE comparison?
steps: Annualised rate of occurrence ARO = 0.2 events per year.
Control cost = ₹60,000 per year; reduced ALE = ₹20,000 per year.
Saving = old ALE − reduced ALE = 50,000 − 20,000 = ₹30,000 per year.
Net = saving − control cost = 30,000 − 60,000 = −₹30,000 per year.
The saving is less than the cost, so the control is not cost-effective by this simple measure.
examples.answer: SLE is ₹2,50,000, ALE is ₹50,000 per year, the yearly saving is ₹30,000, and the net is −₹30,000, so the control is not cost-effective by the simple ALE comparison.

traps: Risk is not the same as a threat or a vulnerability. A threat is what may cause harm; a vulnerability is the weakness; risk combines likelihood and impact.
Compliance with a law or standard does not by itself make a system secure. It proves required paperwork and controls were checked, not that every attack fails.
ALE uses the annualised rate of occurrence, not the exposure factor. SLE uses asset value and exposure factor.
Policy and standard are not interchangeable. A policy states intent; a standard gives a mandatory measurable rule that supports it.

quiz.q: Define policy, standard, procedure and guideline in one line each.
quiz.a: Policy: management statement of intent. Standard: mandatory measurable rule. Procedure: ordered steps to perform work. Guideline: recommended, non-mandatory advice.

quiz.q: Why is risk not the same as a threat?
quiz.a: A threat is a possible cause of harm. Risk also depends on likelihood and impact, so the same threat can give different risk on different assets.

quiz.q: A risk has likelihood 4 and impact 5 on a 1-to-5 scale. What is its score, and what does the score show?
quiz.a: Score = 4 × 5 = 20. It is high risk, close to the maximum 25, so it needs prompt treatment.

quiz.q: An asset is worth ₹8,00,000. Exposure factor is 20% and annualised rate of occurrence is 0.5. Compute SLE and ALE.
A control lowers ALE from ₹80,000 to ₹50,000 per year and costs ₹40,000 per year. Is it cost-effective by the simple ALE comparison? Show the numbers.
quiz.a: Saving = 80,000 − 50,000 = ₹30,000. Net = 30,000 − 40,000 = −₹10,000. The saving is less than the cost, so no by this simple measure.

quiz.q: State one difference between a vulnerability assessment and a penetration test.
quiz.a: A vulnerability assessment finds and lists weaknesses. A penetration test also attempts safe exploitation to show whether weaknesses can be used to reach a goal.

quiz.q: Why does passing a compliance audit not prove that a system is secure?
quiz.a: An audit checks required controls and evidence at a point in time. It cannot prove that every new weakness, misconfiguration or attack path is absent, or that controls still work after changes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry risk teams use quantified methods such as FAIR and continuous control monitoring; cloud providers publish shared-responsibility matrices. Search ISO 27005, the NIST Risk Management Framework and SOC 2 evidence. Only a few universities teach blockchain audit logs, where hash-chained records make tampering visible.
